summary: This document addresses Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) applications that have no capability negotiation, such as those for IP prefixes or point-to-point pseudowires. It describes how to control whether state is advertised when a peer may not use it, to avoid wasted information.

plainLanguage.summary: Some routers send out information that the neighbor does not want. This describes a way to switch that off so they only share what is useful.

questions: what is ldp state advertisement control
how to stop ldp advertising ip prefix labels
what is the ldp sac capability
subtitle: A way for an LDP router to tell its peer which older applications it does not want state for.

tldr.problem: Older LDP applications (IP prefix LSPs and point-to-point pseudowires) have no capability negotiation, so a router can send state its peer does not need, for example IP prefix labels on a session set up only for ICCP or mLDP.
tldr.mechanism: A new State Advertisement Control capability TLV lets a router say, at initialization or later in a Capability message, which of four legacy applications the peer should stop advertising state for.
tldr.outcome: Operators avoid wasted memory, CPU and network resources without hand-built filtering policies. The RFC advises enabling it only by configuration and only when the state is known to be unnecessary.

today: RFC 7473 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 8223.

sections.title: The Problem of Unneeded State
sections.content:
The LDP Capabilities specification (RFC 5561) lets peer Label Switching Routers (LSRs) negotiate features, so that no unnecessary state is exchanged unless a feature is agreed. Newer features such as mLDP and ICCP use it. Earlier LDP applications do not: they exchange state without any capability negotiation.

Two such applications matter here: setting up LSPs for IP unicast prefixes, and signaling L2VPN point-to-point pseudowires. If a session to a remote Provider Edge LSR exists purely for ICCP signaling, the speaker may still advertise labels for IP prefixes to it. On a dual-stack LSR, IPv6 bindings may be sent to a peer that only wants IPv4.

Until now, the RFC says, an operator typically had to configure filtering policies on the LSR to avoid this, which adds overhead and complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a friend who texts you every bit of news about a hobby you do not share. You would like a way to say "only send me the stuff I care about."

sections.title: Non-negotiated Applications and Uninteresting State
sections.content:
The RFC covers the applications that existed before the LDP Capabilities framework. It uses two shorthand names: Prefix-LSPs, which set up LSPs for IP routes by advertising label bindings for Prefix FECs, and P2P-PWs, which signal FEC 128 and FEC 129 L2VPN point-to-point pseudowires.

The state a receiver may be told not to send is called uninteresting state. For Prefix-LSPs it is state related to the IP Prefix FEC, such as label bindings and LDP Status. For P2P-PWs it is state related to the pseudowire FEC, such as label bindings, MAC address withdrawal and PW Status.

One deliberate exception: IP address bindings sent in ADDRESS messages are not uninteresting. An LSR uses peer addresses to map a routing next hop to an LDP peer, and mLDP depends on this, so disabling address bindings would break mLDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The router can say "skip the road maps and the postal notices, but do keep telling me your street address," because it still needs the address to find you.

sections.title: The State Advertisement Control TLV
sections.content:
The new State Advertisement Control (SAC) Capability is a Capability Parameter TLV with type 0x050D. The U-bit MUST be 1, so a receiver that does not know the TLV silently ignores it, and the F-bit MUST be 0. Because the capability cannot be withdrawn once advertised, the S-bit MUST be 1 in both Initialization and Capability messages.

The data is one or more one-byte SAC Elements. Each has a D bit (1 disables state advertisement, 0 enables it; it MUST be 1 in an Initialization message), an App field naming the application, and unused bits that are zero on transmit and ignored on receipt. The TLV Length is 1 plus the number of elements.

A TLV may not repeat an app type. A malformed TLV SHOULD be discarded, and an element with an unknown App value MUST be ignored and discarded while the rest of the TLV is processed. Each incoming element updates the receiver's existing policy for that application.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a tiny form with little tick boxes. Each box names one thing and says "stop sending" or "start sending again."

sections.title: How Peers Handle the Capability
sections.content:
The capability is unilateral and unidirectional: the receiver does not have to send one back. Once it is received and understood, the receiving LSR MUST NOT advertise state for the disabled applications to the sender until they are enabled again. If the update arrives mid-session, the receiver MUST also withdraw any state it advertised earlier for that application.

A speaker that does not understand the TLV MUST answer with an "Unsupported TLV" notification as described in RFC 5561. A speaker that does not support a particular application in an element SHOULD silently skip that element.

The TLV can go in the Initialization message, or later in a Capability message if the peer supports the Dynamic Announcement Capability. Without that support, the alternative is to reset the LDP session so the new capability is sent at the next initialization.
sections.plainLanguage: When your neighbor says "no more flyers," you stop, and you also take back the flyers you already left on their porch.

sections.title: When to Use It
sections.content:
Because disabling label bindings can have wide effects, the RFC says the SAC procedures SHOULD be enabled only through a configuration knob, global or per neighbor, and only toward a neighbor where the advertisement is known to be unnecessary and wasteful.

Typical sessions listed include P2P-PW only (disable IP Prefix LSPs), mLDP-only and ICCP-only (disable IP Prefix LSPs and P2P-PW), and IPv4-only or IPv6-only on a dual-stack LSR (disable the other family's Prefix LSPs, plus P2P-PW).

Cautions: an operator MUST NOT disable Prefix-LSP state on a targeted LDP session used for remote Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) Fast Re-Route, and it is RECOMMENDED not to disable it on tLDP sessions in a remote-LFA network even if the session is PW-only or ICCP-only. To filter only a subset of bindings, the existing filtering procedures should be used, and they may be combined with this capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the "stop sending" switch only when you are sure you never need that news, because some neighbors might one day need it to find a backup route.

sections.title: Operational Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through five cases. On an ICCP session, both LSRs send a SAC TLV with four elements, all with the D-bit set to 1, so neither exchanges Prefix-LSP or P2P-PW state. On a PW tLDP session, they disable only the Prefix-LSPs so that just PW state is exchanged.

For a dynamic change, LSR1 sends a SAC TLV in a Capability message disabling IPv4 and IPv6 Prefix-LSPs; LSR2 stops advertising them and withdraws earlier state, optionally with a single Prefix FEC Typed Wildcard Label Withdraw message if the peer supports it. PW signaling is unaffected.

On an mLDP-only session the peer stops IP Prefix FEC state but still sends the IP address bindings mLDP needs. On a dual-stack LSR, an IPv4-only peer can disable IPv6 Prefix-LSPs and later re-enable them with a Capability message.
sections.plainLanguage: Each example is a different pair of neighbors choosing which kinds of news they want, and changing their minds later without hanging up the phone.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC introduces no new security considerations beyond those of base LDP and of MPLS and GMPLS. For IANA, it registers the State Advertisement Control Capability as TLV type 0x050D in the "TLV Type Name Space" of the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) Parameters registry.
sections.plainLanguage: It does not make anything less safe, and the new tick-box form got its own official number in the big list.

fields.name: U
fields.desc: Must be 1 so unknown receivers silently ignore the TLV.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: 1 plus the number of SAC elements.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Must be 1 in Initialization and Capability messages.

fields.name: SAC Elements
fields.desc: One or more State Advertisement Control Elements (variable length).
